title: How Microsoft’s Principal Software Engineering Manager Works and Uses AI
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Gregor Ojstersek shares a case study from his O'Reilly book The Multiplier Mindset profiling Tarik Guney, a Principal Software Engineering Manager on Microsoft Teams. Guney frames his job as systems thinking: finding where communication delays, unclear processes and misaligned assumptions create bottlenecks, then watching leading indicators rather than only outcomes. He defines multiplying others as raising each person's throughput without raising hours or stress, and breaks that into culture, goals and tooling. His AI use is deliberately layered onto existing workflows, covering meeting summaries, drafting, audience-tailored communication, context reconstruction and routine automation. The pattern across his examples is that AI removes mechanical and cognitive load so the team can spend its energy on framing problems, making decisions and aligning stakeholders. His advice to managers is to start small, solve a real problem today and focus on outcomes over tools. The piece is a practitioner profile rather than a tutorial, and it fits the archive's engineering-leadership thread alongside Ojstersek's other case studies.
points: Guney treats bottlenecks as mostly non-technical, arising from tooling friction, unclear processes and misaligned assumptions that form culture, and he watches leading indicators to catch them early.
He defines multiplying others as increasing throughput without increasing hours or stress, and sorts improvements into culture, goals and tooling because a fix in one rarely helps the others.
Adding a new process to every problem raises cognitive load and limits creativity, so gains stay incremental and local.
AI is used as a layer on existing workflows (notes, drafts, tone checks, context rebuilding) to reduce mechanical load rather than to replace judgment.
His advice to engineering managers is to start small, integrate AI into current workflows and enable teams to use it in ways that improve how they work together.
quotes: Much of his work is about understanding where things typically break down and identifying bottlenecks and constraints within the system.
Work that does not lead to meaningful value is, in practice, busywork. To eliminate busywork, Guney focuses on both leading and lagging indicators.

In practice, trying to solve every problem with a new process makes things more complex. It increases the cognitive load required to remember and follow each set of steps, while also limiting individuals’ creativity.
He likes to remind himself that the whole of a system eventually moves at the speed of its slowest parts. This mental model helps him focus on the right problems.
Guney and his team use AI to reduce cognitive load associated with repetitive or mechanical steps and free them up to focus on framing problems, making decisions, and aligning teams and stakeholders.
Over time, he says, focusing on bottlenecks builds your intuition about where AI is genuinely useful and where it isn’t. That intuition becomes more valuable than chasing every new capability.
Integrate it into your existing workflows instead of creating entirely new ones. And don’t focus on tools, focus on the outcomes you want.
